Stability of learned node importance in citation networks

Results report - Capstone Project Phase B (26-2-R-2). Niran Czuckermann and Shahar Bar. Advisor: Dr. Dvora Toledano-Kitai. Braude College of Engineering. 20 November 2026.

Main findings
  • A Random Forest did not give the most stable ranking in any of the three datasets. In none of the 27 settings (3 datasets x 9) was the primary forest more stable than the best of degree, k-core, closeness and betweenness.
  • Against PageRank, the measure it learns, the result depends on the dataset. In PubMed-Diabetes the forest keeps the top 10 % more stable in 6 of 9 settings; in Cora and CiteSeer it does so in 0 and 0 of 9.
  • The Phase A design copies its input. A forest that gets PageRank as an input and as its target puts 99.5 % or more of its weight on it. That is why the main model has no PageRank input.
  • Closeness should stay. It is the most informative feature in all three datasets; without it the forest predicts PageRank much worse, and in Cora and CiteSeer it is also less stable. The effect on stability is not the same in every dataset.
  • Results do not carry over automatically from one dataset to another. PubMed-Diabetes alone would have given a more favourable picture.

1. The method in one page

Research question (Phase A). Does a Random Forest that combines several centrality measures give node rankings that are more stable under edge noise than any single measure? A ranking is stable if the same papers stay on top when the citation data is incomplete or partly wrong.

The steps in Figure 1, in plain words:

  1. Clean the graph. Every paper is a node, every citation a directed edge (A cites B: A to B). Duplicates, self-citations, unknown papers and citation loops are removed, because a paper can only cite older papers.
  2. Compute five centralities for every paper (Table 1).
  3. Scale them to [0, 1] with a Min-Max scaler that is fitted once, on the original graph, and never again (the "frozen scaler" of Phase A). On a damaged graph a scaled value may fall outside [0, 1]; it is not clipped.
  4. Train the Random Forest on the original graph. Its target is the PageRank of each paper. Two versions are trained: without PageRank among its inputs (the primary model) and with it (the control, see Section 3).
  5. Base scores and ranking. The two forests and the five single centralities each give every paper a score; scores become ranks (1 = most important, equal scores share the mean rank).
  6. Damage the graph in three ways and three sizes (Table 2); repeat 30 times each, which gives 270 damaged graphs.
  7. Re-score every damaged graph: recompute the features, apply the same frozen scaler, apply the same forests (no retraining), and rank again.
  8. Measure how far each new ranking is from the base ranking (Table 3). The method whose ranking moves least is the most stable.
Table 1. The five features (one number per paper).
FeatureWhat it measuresHow it is computed here
Degreedirect citation links(citations given + received) / (N - 1)
Betweennesshow often the paper lies on a shortest path between two othersexact, directed, divided by (N - 1)(N - 2)
Closenesshow quickly the rest of the network reaches the paper through citationsincoming distances with the Wasserman-Faust correction (decision D17)
PageRanka paper is important if important papers cite itdamping 0.85
k-corehow deep the paper sits in a densely connected groupon the undirected graph, without self-loops
Table 2. The three kinds of damage. Each is applied to 5 %, 10 % and 20 % of the citations.
KindWhat happensWhat it imitates
Remove citationsrandom citations are deletedmissing data
Add random citationsrandom citations between any two papers are addedwrong citations (may create impossible loops)
Add citations newer to olderrandom citations are added, but only from a newer to an older paperwrong citations that are still possible in time
Table 3. How the new ranking is compared with the base ranking (every method against its own base ranking).
MeasureQuestion it answersBest value
Spearman (all papers)is the whole order the same? 1 = identical, 0 = unrelated1
Top-10 % stayin what share of the damaged graphs does a top-10 % paper stay in the top 10 %?1
Instability (CV)how much does one paper's score jump across the 30 damaged graphs?0

Spearman over all papers can be flattering for methods with many ties (k-core has about 10 different values), so the top-10 % measure is used next to it: it only looks at the papers that matter. The forests are trained to imitate PageRank, so PageRank is their natural comparison; degree and k-core measure a different kind of importance.

Table 4. The datasets after cleaning. Cleaning removed, in this order: self-citations / edges that closed a citation loop / edges to unknown papers / isolated papers. For PubMed-Diabetes the loop edges are the 11 mutual citations (the higher PubMed id is taken as the newer paper); Cora and CiteSeer have no usable time information, so the fewest edges that leave no loop are removed.

Table 4 and Figure 2 show what the three networks share: they are citation graphs without loops, most papers sit at the end of a citation chain, and a few papers collect many citations. They differ in size and connectivity: PubMed-Diabetes is about seven times larger than Cora and is one connected piece, Cora has 78 and CiteSeer 390 separate pieces. This matters for closeness, which is only defined between papers that can reach each other.

3. Why there are two Random Forests: with and without PageRank

What Phase A said. The feature vector of a paper holds five numbers, including PageRank, and the forest is trained to predict PageRank. PageRank is therefore both an input and the answer.

Why that does not work. A forest that is given the answer as an input learns to copy it. The result is a ranking that is PageRank with a little noise, so comparing its stability with PageRank's tells us nothing about combining several measures. This is what happens in all three datasets (Figure 3): the forest with PageRank puts 99.5 % or more of its weight on that one input.

What we do. We train both. The control forest is Phase A exactly as written. The primary forest is the same forest with PageRank removed from its inputs, so it has to rebuild importance from degree, betweenness, closeness and k-core. The conclusions of this report are drawn from the primary forest; the control is reported to show what the original design does.

Table 5. How well each forest predicts PageRank on papers it was not trained on (80 % train, 20 % test). The last column is the best single centrality on its own (Spearman with PageRank).
DatasetR² with PageRankR² withoutSpearman withSpearman withoutBest single centrality
PubMed-Diabetes1.000.751.000.800.73 (closeness)
Cora0.910.671.000.980.98 (closeness)
CiteSeer0.940.840.960.960.94 (closeness)

Which is better, and why. The primary forest predicts PageRank worse (Table 5), as it must, because it is not given the answer. It is better as a test of the research question, because its stability is free to differ from PageRank's. The control cannot do better than PageRank on average: in Cora and CiteSeer its Spearman is within 0.01 of PageRank's on average, and in PubMed-Diabetes it is 0.06 lower on average and up to 0.14 lower after damage, because a tree cannot predict outside the range it was trained on and many scaled values leave that range once citations are added. Better prediction of PageRank is therefore not the aim; testing a combination of measures is. Whether the same holds for other citation networks is what the three datasets are used for: the control copied its input in all three, so the reason for the primary forest does not depend on the dataset.

4. Experiment results

Every method is compared with its own base ranking after each of the 270 damaged graphs. Figure 4 shows the whole order (Spearman) and Figure 5 shows whether the most important 10 % of the papers stay on top. Methods with many tied scores (k-core, degree) reach 1.0 in the second measure partly because tied papers do not change places.

Against PageRank (Figure 6). In PubMed-Diabetes the primary forest keeps the top 10 % more stable than PageRank in 6 of 9 settings (on average +0.15) while the order over all papers is the same on average (+0.000). In Cora and CiteSeer it is not better: the average differences are -0.010 and -0.003 in Spearman and -0.06 and -0.04 in top-10 % stay.

Table 6 gives the numbers behind the figures for the strongest damage. In every row the best single measure (degree, k-core, closeness or betweenness) is at least as stable as the primary forest in Spearman.

5. Does the forest do better without closeness?

Why we tested it. Closeness is the one feature whose Phase A formula had to be changed (decision D17), and it is the feature the primary forest relies on most. The test removes closeness completely: from the features, from both forests and from the list of single measures. Nothing else changes (same data, same damage, same 30 repeats). The test lives on its own branch and in its own result folders; the main code still computes closeness.

Table 7. What removing closeness changes for the primary forest. The two change columns are averages over the 9 damage settings (negative = less stable without closeness). The last column counts the settings in which the forest keeps the top 10 % more stable than PageRank, with and without closeness.
DatasetCloseness weight in the forestHold-out R²Change in SpearmanChange in top-10 % staySettings better than PageRank
PubMed-Diabetes47 %0.75 to 0.26+0.028-0.0366 to 6 of 9
Cora90 %0.67 to 0.28-0.105-0.0580 to 0 of 9
CiteSeer94 %0.84 to 0.45-0.082-0.0260 to 0 of 9

Accuracy. In all three datasets the forest predicts PageRank clearly worse without closeness (Figure 7): R² falls by 0.49 in PubMed-Diabetes, 0.39 in Cora and 0.38 in CiteSeer. Closeness carries 47 %, 90 % and 94 % of the forest's decisions, and on its own it follows PageRank better than any other single measure.

Stability (Table 7, Figure 8). The effect is not the same in every dataset. In Cora and CiteSeer the forest is less stable without closeness (-0.105 and -0.082 in Spearman) and never beats PageRank. In PubMed-Diabetes the order over all papers is slightly more stable without closeness (+0.028), but the top 10 % is less stable (-0.036). The small gain in PubMed-Diabetes comes with a forest that predicts PageRank far worse (R² 0.26); it leans on degree and k-core, which are stable but measure something else.

Answer to the question
  • Better results without closeness? No for accuracy (all three datasets). For stability it depends on the dataset: worse in Cora and CiteSeer, mixed in PubMed-Diabetes. We do not recommend dropping closeness.
  • The same on other citation networks? The loss of accuracy is the same in all three; the effect on stability is not. A conclusion from one dataset therefore does not carry over, and more datasets would be needed to say how often each case occurs.

6. Answers to the research questions and hypotheses

Table 8. The three Phase A hypotheses, checked on each dataset with the primary forest (averages over the 9 damage settings).
HypothesisPubMed-DiabetesCoraCiteSeer
H1: a combined score is more stable than single measuresvs PageRank: top-10 % stay better in 6 of 9, Spearman better in 3 of 9; vs the best of degree, k-core, closeness and betweenness: better in 0 of 9vs PageRank: top-10 % stay better in 0 of 9, Spearman better in 2 of 9; vs the best of degree, k-core, closeness and betweenness: better in 0 of 9vs PageRank: top-10 % stay better in 0 of 9, Spearman better in 2 of 9; vs the best of degree, k-core, closeness and betweenness: better in 0 of 9
H2: the forest copes with the failure of one feature by using the othersthe control puts 99.8 % on its PageRank input; the primary forest puts 47 % on closenessthe control puts 99.5 % on its PageRank input; the primary forest puts 90 % on closenessthe control puts 99.8 % on its PageRank input; the primary forest puts 94 % on closeness
H3: the network core keeps its high rank (adjusted core rule)core papers stay in the top 10 % in 81 % of the damaged graphs, other important papers in 63 %core papers stay in the top 10 % in 89 % of the damaged graphs, other important papers in 71 %core papers stay in the top 10 % in 84 % of the damaged graphs, other important papers in 72 %

Table 8 answers them with numbers from each dataset. H1 is supported only in a narrow sense: for the top 10 % of PubMed-Diabetes against PageRank. It does not hold in Cora or CiteSeer, and in no dataset is the forest more stable than the best simple measure. H2 is not supported: the Phase A forest copies its PageRank input, and the primary forest depends mostly on one feature, closeness, so a damaged closeness hurts it. H3 holds in all three datasets with the adjusted core rule; the Phase A core rule gives an empty core on this kind of data (decision D16).

7. Limits of these results

  • Three datasets. All are small to medium citation graphs of scientific papers: biomedical papers on diabetes (PubMed-Diabetes), machine-learning papers (Cora) and computer-science papers in six areas (CiteSeer). The differences between them show that one dataset is not enough for a general claim.
  • One target. The forests learn PageRank. Agreeing with PageRank is not the same as measuring true importance, and a ranking can be stable and still wrong.
  • No dates. Citation loops in Cora and CiteSeer were removed with the fewest edges, which is a choice (decision D18); PubMed-Diabetes uses its id order.
  • Forest settings. Every tree sees all features at every split (no feature randomness), which differs from the usual Random Forest and from the argument of Phase A hypothesis H2. A rerun with half the features per split is still open.
  • Trees cannot extrapolate. After citations are added many scaled inputs leave the range seen in training, and the forest gives all those papers the same score. Part of its stability is this effect.
  • Training and testing on the same graph, as in Phase A; the hold-out check only shows that the forest learned something.

Reproducing this report

From the project folder (Python 3.12, packages as in requirements.txt):

CITATION_DATASET=cora FEATURE_SET=full          python scripts/run_pipeline.py   # about 1 minute
CITATION_DATASET=cora FEATURE_SET=no_closeness  python scripts/run_pipeline.py
(the same for citeseer and pubmed; PubMed with all features is notebooks 01-08)
python scripts/build_report.py                  # writes results/report/
